summary: Some DHCP options carry unique identifiers that can enable tracking even when other identifiers are randomized. This standards-track RFC defines anonymity profiles for clients that want to remain anonymous on a visited network, with guidelines on composing DHCP and DHCPv6 messages to minimize identifying information.

plainLanguage.summary:
This RFC tells DHCP clients how to stay anonymous on a network they are only visiting. It lists which DHCP and DHCPv6 options a client should send, which it should leave out, and how to build the ones that stay so that they change whenever the client changes its network address.

The goal is that a network operator cannot tell the same device apart from one visit to the next. The cost is that the client gives up the stable settings that let a server recognize a returning device.

questions: what is the dhcp anonymity profile
why randomize mac address and dhcp identifier
subtitle: How a DHCP client can keep its identity to itself on a network it does not control.

tldr.problem: Randomizing the MAC address is not enough to hide a device on a visited network. DHCP and DHCPv6 messages carry options that name the device, so the same device can still be recognized and followed from one place to the next.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two anonymity profiles, one for DHCPv4 and one for DHCPv6. Each profile lists the options a client may send, which it should leave out, and how to build the ones that stay, so that identifiers change whenever the link-layer address changes.
tldr.outcome: The profiles are guidelines for clients, mainly mobile devices. They trade away the stable parameters that let a server recognize a returning client, and they do nothing about radio fingerprinting, which identifies a device from its radio hardware rather than its addresses.

facts.label: Obfuscated host name
facts.value: Hexadecimal form of the first 6 octets of a hash

today: RFC 7844 is a Proposed Standard from May 2016 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives guidance to DHCP clients, mainly mobile devices, and says nothing about the privacy of DHCP servers, which it leaves for further study.

sections.title: Why a Randomized MAC Address Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The document starts from reports of systems that would monitor the wireless connections of passengers at Canadian airports. The assumption is that such systems are either fragments or trials of a wider system that would monitor Internet users as they move between wireless access points and other temporary attachments, and that privacy-conscious users will try to evade it by randomizing low-level identifiers such as link-layer addresses.

Link-layer addresses are the familiar hardware addresses. Standard Wi-Fi implementations use unique 48-bit addresses assigned according to the IEEE 802 procedures, and the device puts the address in the header of every packet it transmits. Even when the Wi-Fi packets are encrypted, the part of the header carrying the addresses is sent in cleartext, so a tracker can listen to the airwaves and see which devices are nearby. Those addresses can then be correlated with other data, such as names and cookies in cleartext, to build a registry that links an address to the owner of the device. Once that is done, following the address is enough to follow the person, even when all the application data is encrypted. Link-layer addresses can also be correlated with IP addresses, which cancels the privacy benefit of IPv6 privacy addresses.

The obvious response is to replace the MAC address with a randomly drawn 48-bit value before connecting to a network. There is no established standard for doing this yet, and several strategies have been tried: a new random address per connection, a new random address per network, or a new address on a regular time interval. The RFC notes there are many reasons to keep the address constant for the life of a connection, because in Wi-Fi changing it means dropping and re-establishing the connection, which changes the IP addresses, forces every TCP connection to be re-established and restarts NAT traversal. It also makes the change easy to spot, since an observer sees one station leave and another arrive moments later talking to the same IP addresses. The anonymity profiles therefore assume the per-connection or per-network strategies, or a time-interval variant whose interval is about as long as the average connection.

MAC randomization on its own is not enough, because DHCP and DHCPv6 options can carry identifiers of their own. The RFC therefore defines anonymity profiles that describe how to compose DHCP and DHCPv6 messages so that as little identifying information as possible is disclosed.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the Wi-Fi address each time helps, but the DHCP messages that follow still name the device. This RFC works out which DHCP options have to be dropped or rewritten so that the same device cannot be recognized from one visit to the next.

sections.title: Fingerprinting and the Decision Not to Announce Anonymity
sections.content:
Two kinds of fingerprinting are discussed. Radio fingerprinting identifies a radio transmitter by the unique fingerprint of its signal, the tiny differences caused by minute imperfections in the radio transmission hardware. It can be applied to diverse kinds of radio, including Wi-Fi. No amount of link-layer address randomization protects against it. The RFC does not give up on randomization for this reason, since radio fingerprinting is harder to deploy than simply recording addresses with a scanner, and it can only track devices whose fingerprints are already known, so its reach is narrower than mass monitoring of addresses and DHCP parameters. Protections against it may exist but are outside the scope of the document.

Operating system fingerprinting works differently. Where a standard allows several options, different implementers make different choices of which options to support and which values to use, and the order in which options are sent varies too. Watching the options and values present in DHCP messages reveals those differences and allows the type and version of the software on a device to be found. The design of the anonymity profiles tries to reduce the number of options and the choice of values so that fewer such distinctions remain.

Reviewers suggested adding an option that says explicitly that the client is using the anonymity profile, so a willing server could cooperate, or a new kind of DHCP Unique Identifier that changes over time. The RFC rejects this, because the network operator or others with access to the network may be taking part in surveillance, willingly or not, and revealing a preference for anonymity can trigger extra monitoring. The document compares announcing a desire for privacy to wearing a Guy Fawkes mask: when anonymity is required, sticking out of the crowd is a bad idea. The preference for staying unannounced leads the authors to make the mitigation techniques hard to distinguish from ordinary client behaviour wherever possible.

Randomization has downsides. It breaks management procedures that rely on tracking link-layer addresses, and frequent renewal risks exhausting DHCPv4 address pools, raising neighbour discovery traffic and bloating address tables in IPv6. Implementers therefore have to choose the renewal frequency carefully. Static clients, which usually already stand out through their physical connection parameters, are not expected to use the profiles. Mobile clients that care more about privacy than stable parameters may use them together with RFC 7618.
sections.plainLanguage: The profiles do not make a device invisible. A tracker that can measure the exact shape of its radio signal can still recognize it, and the way a client writes its DHCP options can still reveal which operating system it runs. The RFC also refuses to let a client announce that it wants to be anonymous, because that request alone would mark it out.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 Anonymity Profile
sections.content:
Clients using the DHCPv4 profile control the header parameters and limit the number and values of the options they send, depending on the message.

An anonymized DHCPDISCOVER must contain the Message Type option, may contain the Client Identifier option and may contain the Parameter Request List option, and should contain no other option. An anonymized DHCPREQUEST must contain the Message Type option and may contain the Client Identifier and Parameter Request List options. If it answers a DHCPOFFER it must also contain the Server Identifier option and the Requested IP Address option; if it does not answer an offer it may still carry the Requested IP Address option. It should contain no other option. An anonymized DHCPDECLINE must contain the Message Type, Server Identifier and Requested IP Address options, and may contain the Client Identifier option. An anonymized DHCPRELEASE must contain the Message Type and Server Identifier options and may contain the Client Identifier option. An anonymized DHCPINFORM must contain the Message Type option, may contain the Client Identifier and Parameter Request List options, and should contain no other option.

Several header fields and option values need care. The four octets of the Client IP address field (ciaddr) let a server reallocate the address a client used before, so the client should clear the field when it knows the network attachment has changed, and must never include an address obtained with a different link-layer address. The Requested IP Address option, code 50, is a convenience that risks disclosing an address used at a previous location, so the client should not use it in DHCPDISCOVER but must use it when the protocol mandates it, for example in DHCPREQUEST. A client in the INIT-REBOOT state that wants privacy should perform a complete four-message handshake starting with a DHCPDISCOVER instead of trying to reclaim the old address, unless it is sure it is the same network and the link-layer address has not changed.

The sixteen octets of the Client hardware address field (chaddr) are needed for the service to work, and the client should use the new randomized value when the hardware address has been reset. The Client Identifier option, code 61, exists to identify a client independently of its link-layer address, which is exactly what makes it useful for tracking. In direct conflict with RFC 4361, a client using the anonymity profile must build the client identifier solely from the link-layer address that will be used on the underlying connection, so that it leaks nothing that is not already available to anyone watching the connection, and so that a randomized link-layer address is not cancelled out. Where the underlying connection is a point-to-point link with no link-layer address, the client should pick a random identifier that is highly likely to be unique to the current link, for example a combination of a local secret and an identifier of the connection.

The Parameter Request List option, code 55, lists what the client wants from the server. Different implementations ask for different parameters in different orders, and that choice can be used to fingerprint the client, so a privacy-minded client should ask for a minimal number of options and shuffle their order. If random ordering is not possible, it may order them by option code number from lowest to highest. The same advice applies to the ordering of options in the message as a whole.

Several options are dropped or rewritten. The Host Name option, code 12, carries either a fully qualified domain name such as node1984.example.com or a simple name such as node1984; both are identifying, so the client should not send it, and if it does send it the name must be unqualified and obfuscated. A suggested construction is to hash a local secret together with the link-layer address and use the hexadecimal form of the first six octets of the hash, though the RFC notes that this pattern is itself recognizable and is only a suggestion. The Client FQDN option, code 81, lets the client advertise its domain name so the server can update DNS; the client should not include it, though it may use a special-purpose FQDN built from the same obfuscated host name plus the connection-specific DNS suffix the server advertised. The UUID/GUID-based Client Machine Identifier option, code 97, carries a 16-octet GUID that uniquely identifies the device; since it belongs to the pre-boot environment, nodes visiting untrusted networks must not send or use the PXE options. Finally, the Vendor-Specific Information option (code 43), the Vendor Class Identifier option (code 60), the V-I Vendor Class option (code 124) and the V-I Vendor-Specific Information option (code 125) should all be left out, because they can reveal identifying information.
sections.plainLanguage: A client using the profile sends only the options it truly needs: the message type, and at most a client identifier and a list of requested parameters. Host names, domain names, vendor options and pre-boot identifiers are left out. The client identifier, if sent, is built from the link-layer address rather than from a permanent hardware number, so it changes whenever the address changes.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 Anonymity Profile
sections.content:
DHCPv6 clients are in one of two situations. In the stateful one they use Solicit, Request, Confirm, Renew, Rebind, Release and Decline messages to obtain and manage addresses. In the stateless one they configure addresses themselves from client-managed identifiers and router-advertised prefixes, and use DHCPv6 only for network configuration parameters through the Information-request message. Where a router advertisement enables stateless address configuration, hosts using the anonymity profile should use it, because stateless configuration requires fewer disclosures than stateful configuration.

The client identifier option, code 1, carries a DHCP Unique Identifier, and a stable DUID is the main privacy concern in DHCPv6. With randomized link-layer addresses the client must use DUID format number 3, link-layer address, with the value currently assigned to the interface. Without the benefit of randomized link-layer addresses, a privacy-minded client should generate a new randomized DUID-LLT every time it attaches to a new link or detects a possible link change; the DUID type should be 1, the hardware type should match, the embedded link address should be randomized, and the time should be a random timestamp from the previous year. A current timestamp would reveal that the identifier was newly generated and so would give away information for device fingerprinting. The RFC also notes that a client is allowed to omit its client identifier in an Information-request message, and clients using stateless DHCPv6 who want privacy should do exactly that, accepting that the server can no longer send them client-specific options.

The Server Identifier option, code 2, should be used as specified, but the client must only include server identifier values it received with the current link-layer address, because reusing old values gives away information. The option request option, code 6, has the same problem as the DHCPv4 parameter request list: the choice and order of requested options can fingerprint the client, so only a minimal subset should be requested and the order should be shuffled, falling back to ordering by option code number. A client may also include the requested options themselves as hints of the values it would like; clients using the profile should not, because the old values might identify the client.

For addresses, the IA_NA option, code 3, is used for non-temporary addresses. Its IAID parameter must not enable client identification, and while it must be consistent across restarts of the client, the RFC reads that as requiring it to be constant for the association as long as the link-layer address stays constant. One construction is to combine one octet of interface number with the first three octets of the link-layer address. The IA Address option, code 5, may be used, but the client has to weigh the advantage of address continuity against the risk of disclosing a previous address; a solution is to drop all stored addresses when the link-layer address changes and to use the option only for addresses explicitly assigned through the current link-layer address. The IA_TA option, code 4, for temporary addresses, should not be used: the feature is not widely used, no lifetime or lease length is specified for it, so renewal support varies and may be absent, and asking for it reveals the desire for privacy. The addresses obtained as non-temporary addresses are used as temporary ones by the profile and are discarded when the link-layer address changes.

Prefix delegation, which uses IA_PD, has similar anonymity properties. Clients that desire anonymity and never request more than one prefix should set the IAID to zero, as authorized in Section 6 of RFC 3633, and should not document any previously assigned prefix in the IA_PD Prefix option. Requesting a prefix at all is a form of fingerprinting while client use of prefix delegation is still uncommon.

Three more options are ruled out. The Authentication option, code 11, exists to authenticate clients and servers and so can identify the client, which conflicts with the goal; clients using the profile should not use it, though they may in a trusted environment such as a workplace network. The User Class option, code 15, and the Vendor Class option, code 16, should not be used because they can reveal identifying information. The Client FQDN option, code 39, should not be included, because it identifies the client, though a local-only FQDN combining a host name derived from the link-layer address with a suffix advertised by the local DHCPv6 server may be used.

One message is treated specially. RFC 3315 requires clients to send a Confirm message when they attach to a new link, to check whether the configuration they already hold is still valid. The Confirm message carries the identity associations and addresses from the previous link, so an attacker can trivially learn the previous point of attachment. Clients interested in privacy should not send Confirm messages and should instead try to acquire addresses on the new link directly, accepting that this can cause a connectivity hiatus when roaming between two access points in the same wireless network. Clients that can verify that the previous and current links belong to the same network may still send Confirm messages; the most reliable way to detect attachment is through link-layer security such as IEEE 802.1X.
sections.plainLanguage: The DHCPv6 profile follows the same idea: send only what is needed, and make every identifier change when the network address changes. That means a fresh client identifier on each new link, no Confirm message, no domain name, no class options, and a stable address only while the link-layer address stays the same.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Hiding the client identity from the DHCP server is not always desirable. Some servers publish names and addresses in DNS, or make sure that returning clients get the same address again. Clients using an anonymity profile may also consume more resources: when a client changes its link-layer address and requests a new IP address, the old address is still marked as leased by the server.

Some DHCP servers only give addresses to pre-registered MAC addresses, which forces such clients to choose between remaining anonymous and obtaining connectivity at all. Because of this, implementers should provide a way for clients to control when the anonymity profiles are used and when standard behaviour is preferred. One option is to tie the use of the profiles to the use of link-layer address randomization.
sections.plainLanguage: An anonymous client cannot expect a server to remember it, and it may leave stale addresses behind in the server's pool. Some servers will not serve a device at all unless its hardware address is registered, so a client needs a way to turn the profile on and off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states in one sentence that using the anonymity profiles does not change the security considerations of DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 as defined in RFC 2131 and RFC 3315. It adds no new requirements of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The profiles do not add or remove any security rules for DHCP itself. They only change which options a client sends.

viz.caption: What a DHCP exchange can reveal about the device that sent it

items.title: Link-layer address
items.text: 48 bits sent in cleartext in the header of every Wi-Fi frame.

items.title: DHCP client identifier
items.text: A stable value that lets a server recognize the same device again.

items.title: Requested IP address
items.text: An address used at a previous location, which shows where the device has been.

items.title: Host name and FQDN
items.text: Often unique in a large network, and easy to tie to a person.

items.title: Vendor and user class
items.text: Say which make and model of equipment is on the network.

items.title: Option order and values
items.text: Differences between implementations reveal the operating system and version.

viz.caption: What address randomization does and does not hide

left.title: Randomized link-layer address
left.desc: The device presents a random 48-bit address for the connection, so the same address is not seen twice.

right.title: Radio fingerprint
right.desc: The unique signature of the radio hardware identifies the device whatever address it chooses to use.

viz.caption: The DHCPv4 options the profile has something to say about

items.label: Host Name
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be sent. If sent, the name must be unqualified and obfuscated.

items.label: Requested IP Address
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used in DHCPDISCOVER, but MUST be used where the protocol requires it.

items.label: Parameter Request List
items.desc: SHOULD ask for a minimal set of options and shuffle their order.

items.label: Client Identifier
items.desc: MUST be based solely on the link-layer address used on the underlying connection.

items.label: Client FQDN
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be included; a local-only FQDN may be used instead.

items.label: UUID/GUID Client Machine Identifier
items.desc: Carries a 16-octet GUID. MUST NOT be sent or used on untrusted networks.

items.label: Vendor options
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used, because they can reveal identifying information.

viz.caption: The DHCPv6 options the profile has something to say about

items.label: Client Identifier
items.desc: Holds a DUID. With randomized addresses use format 3, link-layer address; otherwise a fresh random DUID-LLT per link.

items.label: Server Identifier
items.desc: Only values received with the current link-layer address may be included.

items.label: Option Request
items.desc: Request a minimal subset of options and shuffle their order.

items.label: Authentication
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used, because the option can identify the client.

items.label: User Class and Vendor Class
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used, because they can reveal identifying information.

items.label: Client FQDN
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be included; a local-only FQDN may be used instead.
